findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit a request context that is canceled when the response returns
findings.body: Each secondary write derives its timeout context from the request context. For incoming HTTP requests, that parent context is canceled when the handler returns, which is exactly when mode 3 returns success to the caller. The legacy Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection can therefore start with, or become interrupted by, context.Canceled and silently fail after the unified write has succeeded. Detach cancellation while retaining values (for example, use context.WithoutCancel before applying the 10-second timeout) so the shadow write has its intended lifetime.

findings.title: Independent async writes can reach legacy storage in a different order than unified storage
findings.body: There is no ordering or serialization for the background legacy operations. For example, a successful unified Create can enqueue its legacy create, then a client can successfully Delete the same object; if the legacy delete runs first it sees NotFound and is ignored, and the delayed create then recreates the object in legacy storage. Mode 3 continues reading unified storage, so this divergence is hidden until a rollback or mode change resurrects stale data. Secondary operations need ordered, per-object delivery (and appropriate handling for collection operations), rather than one unconstrained goroutine per primary write.

findings.title: Legacy update re-evaluates the original updater instead of replicating the primary result
findings.body: Storage.Update has already invoked objInfo to produce res, but the asynchronous Legacy.Update receives the original objInfo and invokes it again against legacy storage's old object. UpdatedObjectInfo is a transformation over the current object and may contain patch/apply behavior, resource-version checks, or other non-idempotent logic; legacy can therefore reject the update or persist a result different from the unified result when the stores are even slightly out of sync. The secondary write should be wrapped to return the successful primary result (as the previous updateWrapper-based implementation did), rather than reapplying the client updater.

findings.title: A primary NotFound delete no longer attempts legacy cleanup
findings.body: Any Storage.Delete error now returns before scheduling the legacy delete, including NotFound. This leaves a stale legacy object permanently after a prior asynchronous legacy delete timed out or failed: retrying the delete returns NotFound from unified storage and never repairs legacy storage. On a rollback to legacy reads, the supposedly deleted object reappears. Preserve the prior special handling that still issues the legacy delete for an apierrors.IsNotFound primary result while returning the primary NotFound response to the caller.

findings.title: Destroy can tear down storage while background legacy calls are still running
findings.body: Mode 3 returns before its secondary goroutines complete, but Destroy immediately calls Legacy.Destroy and Storage.Destroy without waiting for them. During server shutdown, a goroutine can consequently call Legacy.Create/Update/Delete after Legacy.Destroy has closed its client or other resources, losing the copy and potentially racing with teardown. Track outstanding secondary work and drain or cancel-and-wait for it before destroying either backend.

findings.title: Every successful write can create an unbounded ten-second goroutine
findings.body: Each successful primary mutation starts a new goroutine that can remain blocked in the legacy backend for up to ten seconds (or longer if that backend does not honor context cancellation). During a legacy outage, write traffic can accumulate an unbounded number of goroutines and request objects, causing scheduler and memory pressure while the primary path continues accepting writes. Use a bounded worker queue or other admission-controlled replication mechanism; it can also provide the ordering needed for consistent legacy state.

findings.title: Delete duration metrics use the object name as the resource label
findings.body: The successful delete path passes name to recordStorageDuration where every other operation passes options.Kind. Object names are user-controlled and effectively unbounded, so this creates a distinct Prometheus time series for each deleted object instead of aggregating by resource kind. Besides making the metric semantically wrong, sustained deletes can cause unbounded metrics cardinality and memory use. Pass options.Kind here.

findings.title: Several primary and legacy timings are recorded to the wrong metric family
findings.body: A failed Storage.Create is recorded with recordLegacyDuration at line 45, and a failed Storage.Update does the same at line 129, even though no legacy operation was attempted. Conversely, the legacy DeleteCollection call records recordStorageDuration at line 166. This reports primary failures as legacy failures and double-counts storage timings while omitting legacy timing, making migration health alerts and dashboards misleading. Use the storage recorder for primary calls and the legacy recorder for secondary calls.

findings.title: The new mode-3 integration scenario assumes legacy replication is synchronous
findings.body: The mode-3 subtest calls doPlaylistTests, which performs K8s mutations and then immediately asserts that legacy playlist endpoints return the same data. Mode 3 intentionally returns before the legacy write completes, so a valid slow scheduler or legacy backend can make these assertions intermittently see NotFound or stale data. The test needs an eventual assertion or an explicit test-visible replication completion signal before checking legacy state; otherwise it will be flaky and cannot reliably validate asynchronous replication.
